speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Good afternoon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I remain squarely focused on achieving our dual-mandate goals of maximum employment and stable prices for the benefit of the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The U.S. economy has been expanding at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: While job gains have remained low, the unemployment rate has been little changed in recent months, and inflation remains somewhat elevated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Today, the FOMC decided to leave our policy rate unchanged.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We see the current stance of monetary policy as appropriate to promote progress toward our maximum-employment and 2 percent inflation goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The implications of developments in the Middle East for the U.S. economy are uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will remain attentive to risks to both sides of our dual mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I’ll have more to say about monetary policy after briefly reviewing economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Available indicators suggest that economic activity has been expanding at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Consumer spending has been resilient, and business fixed investment has continued to expand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In contrast, activity in the housing sector has remained weak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our Summary of Economic Projections, the median participant projects that real GDP will rise 2.4 percent this year and 2.3 percent next year, somewhat stronger than projected in December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the labor market, the unemployment rate was 4.4 percent in February and has changed little since late last summer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Job gains have remained low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A good part of the slowing in the pace of job growth over the past year reflects a decline in the growth of the labor force due to lower immigration and labor force participation, though labor demand has clearly softened as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Other indicators, including job openings, layoffs, hiring, and nominal wage growth, generally show little change in recent months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our SEP, the median projection of the unemployment rate is 4.4 percent at the end of this year and edges down thereafter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased significantly from its highs in mid-2022 but remains somewhat elevated relative to our 2 percent longer-run goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Estimates based on the consumer price index and other data indicate that total PCE prices rose 2.8 percent over the 12 months ending in February and that, excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core PCE prices rose 3.0 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: These elevated readings largely reflect inflation in the goods sector, which has been boosted by the effects of tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Near-term measures of inflation expectations have risen in recent weeks, likely reflecting the substantial rise in oil prices caused by the supply disruptions in the Middle East.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Most measures of longer-term expectations remain consistent with our 2 percent inflation goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median projection in the SEP for total PCE inflation this year is 2.7 percent and 2.2 percent next year, a bit higher than projected in December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our monetary policy actions are guided by our dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At today’s meeting, the Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3½ to 3¾ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: From last September through December, we lowered our policy rate ¾ percentage point, bringing it within a range of plausible estimates of neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This normalization of our policy stance should continue to help stabilize the labor market while allowing inflation to resume its downward trend toward 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the implications of events in the Middle East for the U.S. economy are uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the near term, higher energy prices will push up overall inflation, but it is too soon to know the scope and duration of the potential effects on the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will continue to monitor the risks to both sides of our mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are well positioned to determine the extent and timing of additional adjustments to our policy rate based on the incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our SEP, FOMC participants wrote down their individual assessments of an appropriate path of the federal funds rate under what each participant judges to be the most likely scenario for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median participant projects that the appropriate level of the federal funds rate will be 3.4 percent at the end of this year and 3.1 percent at the end of next year, unchanged from December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As is always the case, these individual forecasts are subject to uncertainty, and they are not a Committee plan or decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Monetary policy is not on a preset course, and we’ll make our decisions on a meeting-by-meeting basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: To conclude: The Fed has been assigned two goals for monetary policy—maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We remain committed to supporting maximum employment, bringing inflation sustainably to our 2 percent goal, and keeping longer-term inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our success in delivering on these goals matters to all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We at the Fed will continue to do our jobs with objectivity, integrity, and a deep commitment to serve the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I look forward to your questions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So first let me say, we’re well aware of the performance of inflation over the last few years and how a series of shocks have interrupted progress that we’ve made over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that happened most recently with tariffs, and then—and now there will be some effects on inflation coming forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The, the thing that’s really important that we see this year is progress on inflation through a reduction in goods inflation as the one-time effects on prices of tariffs go through the system—go through the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s the main thing we’re looking for, going into this exercise.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we need to be seeing that to, you know, to sort of understand that we actually are making progress because, on net, we didn’t make progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And if you look at total inflation—sorry, total core inflation, it’s about 3 percent, and some big chunk of that, between a half and three-quarters, is actually tariffs, so we’re looking for progress on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The question of whether we “look through” the energy inflation doesn’t really arise until we have kind of checked that box.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It, of course, is kind of standard learning that you “look through” energy shocks, but that’s always been dependent on inflation expectations remaining well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think now it’s also dependent now on what you mentioned, which is that broader context of five years now of inflation above target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have to keep all of those things in mind, and the question of “looking through,” when it does arise, will be one to approach not lightly but, you know, in the context that you mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, so there are 19 people and so 19 reasons, 19 individual submissions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, but, but—and if you notice, the median didn’t change, but there was actually some movement toward—a meaningful amount of movement toward, toward fewer cuts by people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So four or five people went from two to one, let’s say—two cuts to one cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And each person has individual, you know, stories behind what they want to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But essentially it is that, you know, the, the forecast is that we’ll be making progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Not as much as we had hoped, but some progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It should come as we start to see in the middle of the year progress on tariffs going through once and then tariff inflation coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s—we should be seeing that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the rate forecast is conditional on the performance of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So if we don’t see that progress, then you won’t see the rate cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s going to be part of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the oil shock for sure shows up here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Some of that will be in core as well, but yes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, no, there’s also just the feeling that we haven’t seen the progress that we had hoped for on core goods and on tariffs and on the rest of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’ve, we’ve—so for whatever reason people did write up their inflation forecast, that will certainly be tied to events in the Middle East and the price of oil, but it’s also, I think, a reflection of the slow progress we’ve seen on tariffs—which we believe we will see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s just a question of how long it takes for them to get all the way through the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it takes—it just takes some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I, I didn’t get the second part of your question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the thing I really want to emphasize is that nobody knows.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The economics effect could be bigger, they could be smaller, they could be much smaller or much bigger.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We just don’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So people are writing down something that seems to make sense to them but have no conviction that’s—to your point, if we have high—if we have a long period of much higher gas prices, that’s going to weigh on consumption, that will weigh on disposable personal income, and it’ll weigh on consumption.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we don’t know if that’s going to happen—something quite different from that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We might have much lower-than-expected pass-through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So people write down—this is one of those SEPs where a number of people mentioned if we were ever going to skip an SEP, this would be a good one, because we just don’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I wouldn’t say there’s a conviction that this is going to go through quickly, or not quickly, it just—you’ve got to write something down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And this is something that is—that people wrote down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so—and we don’t debate how long.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We wouldn’t be able to debate what the length or size of these effects would be—we just have to kind of make an individual statement.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And also what you’ve written down before will be—you’ll be reluctant to move too far away from that, just because you don’t know—it’s so unclear what the direction from this particular end will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Meanwhile, the economy has—growth has been solid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And inflation—the overshoot is mainly from the goods [sector] and tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the labor market is—the unemployment rate, of course, is little changed since September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You have a very, very low breakeven rate, apparently, for new jobs, with little growth in either demand or supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the U.S. economy is doing pretty well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s just, we don’t know what the effects of this will be, and really no one does.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the first thing is, there is the original thinking—the long-standing thinking, put it that way, is that you do “look through” energy shocks, but, as I mentioned, that’s conditioned on inflation expectations and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s, that’s true.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So any, any effects on employment and economic activity in spending would be offset to some extent by the fact that our, our oil companies will be more profitable, and they may even do more drilling.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you ask oil companies about doing more drilling, though, they’re going to want to see a consistent rise in oil prices from where they were before the buildup for the war.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And they’re going to want to believe that that’s going to be persistent for a fairly long time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So they’re, they’re not sitting there waiting for oil to go over $70 a barrel and then they’re going to start drilling or whatever.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re going to make a reasoned, careful judgment that we’re going to have higher oil prices for an extended period of time—meaningfully higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you don’t—I wouldn’t say there’s much of that happening, not much happening now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But some of that could happen over time if you see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So they’re—the net—the net of it—the net of the oil shock will still be some downward pressure on spending and employment and upward pressure on inflation, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we have to do our analysis and think these things through carefully, but of course that’s on everyone’s mind.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re well aware of the history and—but you don’t want to overreact to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You want to make the best judgment you can based on the facts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t think we’re going to let it color our decisionmaking more than is appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s more the thought that it’s been five years, and we’ve actually had—we had the tariff shock, we had the pandemic, and now we have an energy shock of some size and duration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t know what that’s going to be actually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s one of those things where it’s, it’s a repeated set of things, and you worry that that’s the kind of thing that can, can, you know, cause trouble for inflation expectations, and so we worry a lot about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re—we are very strongly committed to doing what it takes to keep inflation expectations anchored at 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think it’s important that we—that we do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Very important.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Okay.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I would say the rate is—you can characterize it as in the high end of neutral, or you can characterize it as perhaps mildly restrictive, even modestly restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No one knows for sure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s in that range where it’s somewhere around the borderline between restrictive and not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Remember that a big part of the disinflation we’re looking for is just the runoff of—when tariffs are put into place, of course what they do is they raise prices to some extent, to the extent those prices are—the tariffs are paid by consumers on a one-time basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re waiting for that, that process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It takes 8, 9, 10, 11 months—a year—to go through the system.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re waiting for the tariffs, which were put in place over the course of the middle part and later last year, we’re waiting for that to go through the system so that goods inflation will return closer to what it’s always been.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, it used to be—for many, many years it was negative, and then the year before tariffs came in it was zero.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s running at, like, 2 percent now, so, so that’s kind of—goods inflation is running at 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s not coming from standard, Phillips-curve, restrictive, restrictive policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s coming from the runoff of a one-time thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We also think it’s important, though, to keep policy either mildly restrictive or close to that, but not too restrictive because of the weakness in—the downside risk in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are balancing these two goals in a situation where the risks to the labor market are to the downside—which would call for lower rates—and the risks to inflation are to the upside—which would call for higher rates, or not cutting, anyway.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re in a difficult situation, and we feel like we’re—our framework calls on us to balance the risks, and we feel like where we are now, which is kind of on that borderline—the higher borderline of restrictive versus not restrictive, we feel like that’s the right place to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s a good question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s, you know, it’s frustrating.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Labor—nonhousing services [price increases] have, they’ve basically moved sideways for a year, they’re at the same level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we do expect that they will come down, but it’s a bunch of idiosyncratic things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But at the same time, that is one of the things we should be seeing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Because, to your point, you know, the labor market is clearly not a source of inflationary pressures, and that should really matter for nonhousing services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we’re not seeing progress there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we do—what we expect for next year is continued—what we want to see for this year, rather, is continued progress on housing services, finally seeing the goods inflation come back down, because the one-time effects of tariffs are through, and then also get some help from nonhousing services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what we’d like to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s, you know, it’s a good question why we didn’t see much of that last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it’s really—I wouldn’t say that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t say that that’s clear at all, that one is more at risk than the other.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you can—you can point to the unemployment rate being stable, and in a world where both supply and demand for workers have come down very, very sharply over the course of the past year due to immigration policy largely, you know, a ratio is going to be a better thing to look at than job creation, for example.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the ratio is the unemployment rate, and it’s been stable since September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that, that tells you that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation, you know, you can—you can—we’re at 3.0 percent core inflation, 2.8 percent headline, so we’ve been well above 2 percent, that amount, whatever it is, 0.7, 0.8, we’re a full percentage point above 2 percent for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s a concern.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We need to get back down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we need to keep focused on that, even though we do now face some new inflation from energy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I’d be hard pressed to say that one of them is obviously more at risk than the other.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So if my successor is not confirmed by the end of my term as Chair, I would serve as Chair pro tem until he is confirmed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That is what the law calls for, that’s what we’ve done on several occasions—including involving me—and that’s what we’re going to do in this situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And while I’m at it, on the question whether I will leave while the investigation is ongoing: I have no intention of leaving the Board until the investigation is well and truly over, with transparency and finality, and I would refer you to the statement that was in the Fed’s brief that you all have seen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I won’t have anything more for you on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: On the question of whether I will then continue to serve as a Governor after my term ends and after the investigation is over, I have not made that decision yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I will make that decision based on what I think is best for the institution and for the people we serve—figuring you probably were going to set the dominoes off there, Edward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I’m not going to have any more to say on those issues, by the way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we—it’s really hard to say until we see the situation, the actual situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In some circumstances that might be the right case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In fact, for example, if we do see the kinds of disinflationary progress that we expect to see with—due to tariffs that I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think it’s hard to say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it will depend, to some extent, on the size and duration of the effects we’re seeing on prices, and it will depend a lot on what we can see in inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think you have to take the two together.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In a way, the January report was a positive surprise, and the February report was a negative surprise.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you put them together, you get something in the middle, and I think you have to really be—as you do, I’m sure, realize there was a strike and there was weather, and that’s about 80,000 of the negative effect total on the February report.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There are a number of indicators that suggest a degree of stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the thing that I think a good number of the people on the Committee are concerned about is just the very, very low level of job creation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you adjust what has been the trend job creation over the past, let’s say, six months, if you adjust that for what we think, our staff thinks, is the overstatement due to overcounting, effectively there’s zero net job creation in the private sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But actually that looks like that’s about what the economy needs in terms of dealing with very, very low—nonexistent, really—growth in the labor force, which, of course, we’ve never had in our history.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’ve got a sort of a zero employment growth equilibrium.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now that’s balance, okay, but I would say it does have a feel of downside risk, and it’s not kind of a really comfortable balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we look at that, we see it, we get it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, everybody understands the arithmetic and that’s—you can say the breakeven is zero.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, nonetheless, it’s, it’s something we’re watching carefully and are concerned about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But ultimately, though, you can argue that it’s a consequence of deliberate policy, which is really the changes to immigration—that’s the biggest factor there—but, nonetheless, something we watch carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we did go through a long period where the shocks were all demand shocks, and so we’ve had a lot of practice thinking about supply shocks in the last four or five years, for sure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s just a very different thing—much more difficult thing—because it does immediately raise the question of tension between the two parts of our mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This energy supply shock is a one-time thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not—it’s not because of some broad tendency or anything, I don’t think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the oil shock under—with Ukraine was also a consequence of military action.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I don’t know that—I don’t know that the world has changed in a way that there’ll be more supply shocks, but there’s—people have written that paper and that speech a number of times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A number of people have tried to make the case that that is the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, in fact, we have seen more supply shocks in the last five years than we’ve seen in many years before that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a fact.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What happened about that was not much, and I’ll tell you why.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, we, we looked carefully at many aspects of the SEP and of our communications, and there just weren’t—there weren’t any ideas that had very broad support on the Committee.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you don’t want to make a change to your communications unless you have, have the Committee behind that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we didn’t really make any changes on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I had hoped—had some things that I wanted to do, but they just—they didn’t attract broad support, and we’d already made all the changes we made to the framework—that was a critical thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we didn’t.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I wish we had been able to do some things, but we didn’t.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So maybe the next Chair will take a look.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m sure he will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it did come up today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The policy that our—the possibility, rather, that our next move might be an increase did come up at the meeting, as it did at the last meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The vast majority of participants don’t see that as their base case, and, of course, we don’t take things off the table.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But you correctly characterized what was in the minutes—that several participants indicated something very much like that conversation did happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we—you can—you can worry about other commodities, you can worry about all of the ways that oil commodities, oil-related commodities go into manufacturing, that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The truth is, it’s completely out of our hands, and we just, like everybody else, we have to just wait and see what happens.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’ll be—it’ll come down to how long, you know, the current situation lasts, and then what are the effects on prices and then how do consumers react and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Really, we—I wouldn’t speculate in any way, and there’s really not a lot we can do other than kind of watch and see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So at this meeting—I mean, a number of people mentioned, and staff briefed on, short-term expectations having moved up quite a lot for reasons we understand well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
